place.name: The Frick Collection
place.prompt:
The visitor is at The Frick Collection, in Henry Clay Frick's former house at 1 East 70th Street, on Fifth Avenue between 70th and 71st Streets in New York City. Thomas Hastings of Carrère and Hastings designed the house, completed in 1914, as Frick's home, and Frick intended it to become a public museum for his art collection. Frick died in the house on December 2, 1919. After his wife Adelaide died in 1931, John Russell Pope converted the house into a museum, which opened on December 16, 1935. The house closed for renovation from 2020 to 2025 (the collection was shown at Frick Madison, 945 Madison Avenue, from 2021 to 2024) and reopened on April 17, 2025, with an addition designed by Annabelle Selldorf.

The collection is best known for European paintings from the Renaissance to the 19th century, including works by Vermeer, Rembrandt, Holbein, Bellini, Titian, El Greco, Velázquez, Goya, Fragonard, Gainsborough and Turner, shown in the rooms of the house alongside sculpture, furniture, porcelain, enamels, portrait medals, and clocks and watches.

The first floor held the family's shared rooms and the second floor their bedrooms and private rooms; both are now galleries. First floor: Entrance Hall (Room 1), East Vestibule (3), Octagon Room (4), Anteroom (5), Cabinet (6), Dining Room (7), West Vestibule (8), Fragonard Room (9), Living Hall (10), Library (11), Portico Gallery (12), West Gallery (13), Enamels Room (14), Oval Room (15), East Gallery (16), Garden Court (17), North Hall (18), South Hall (19), Foot of Stairs and Landing (20), and the Ronald S. Lauder Exhibition Galleries for special exhibitions. Second floor: Grand Stair Hall (21), Long Hall (22), Medals Room (23), Sitting Room (24), Walnut Room (25), Gold-Grounds Room (26), Ceramics Room (27), Boucher Anteroom (28), Boucher Room (29), Du Paquier Passage (30), Small Hallway (31), Impressionist Room (32), Clocks and Watches Room (33), Breakfast Room (34) and Lajoue Passage (35). The Frick Art Research Library, founded by Helen Clay Frick in 1920, is part of the institution.

Henry Clay Frick (1849–1919) made his fortune in coke and steel. His career includes the violent 1892 Homestead Strike at Carnegie Steel, and he was a founding member of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club, whose dam failed in 1889, causing the Johnstown Flood.
